units.translation: Will you not be silent and say none of these things throughout the city?
Silence! Who cries out, struck with a mortal blow?
Or shall I go in silence, having poured out these libations dishonorably, a drink not to be drunk?
Gellius 13, 19, 4 cites almost the same words from the Prometheus the Fire-Bearer (fr. 188).
It is not possible for me either to be silent or not to be silent about these fortunes.
But it is a pain to be silent.
Do not think that I am silent out of luxury or self-will.
But I am silent about these things.
But yours again is the silence.
Will you not endure these things in silence to your ruin?
I am silent; with others I will suffer what is fated.
He loves to be silent or to speak what is timely.
I have long been silent, unhappy one.
But the rest I keep silent.
Not even if she is silent is there envy.
Long have I held silence as a remedy for harm.
To be silent where one must and to speak what is timely.
I know how to speak where it is right, and likewise to be silent.
The axle-driven pipes do not keep silent.

In a corrupt passage, in which only this much seems certain, that it has been rightly corrected to σιγὰς ἀτίμους ἀλοιδόρους [dishonored silences, not reviled] or σιγὰς ἀτίμως ἀλοιδόρως [silences dishonorably, not revilingly], about which I have spoken in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. XCI.
For to many mortals silence is a gain.
to come to the iron-mother land
directing with iron, distributing with iron
directing with iron, distributing with iron
Iron-struck indeed are they here, and iron-struck await those.
(and in Doric σίδαρος in lyric passages) iron
bronze, iron (σίδαρος M), silver, and gold.
they divided by lot with the hammered Scythian iron the whole property.
Why then (thus Lachmann for ἤδη) have you been reconciled with iron?
the sea-born stranger, hastening from fire, sharpened iron
And the iron-workers, the Chalybes, dwell on the left hand.
For an iron-hearted spirit, blazing with courage, breathed.

Sidonian, an adjective derived from Σιδών [Sidon], which was a city of Phoenicia. The common form is Σιδώνιος [Sidonian], for which Σιδόνιος [Sidonian] Homer and other poets said for the sake of meter: see Thes. vol. 7 p. 232.
with linen or a Sidonian veil
the smooth fields of Sicily rich in fair fruit

With this accent M: in the copies Σιληνίων [of the Silenians]. The scholiast: Σιληνίαι αἰγιαλός Σαλαμίνος, πλησίον τῆς λεγομένης Τροπαίου ἄκρας, ὡς Τιμόξενος ἐν τῷ ς΄ περὶ λιμένων [Sileniae is a shore of Salamis, near the so-called Cape of the Trophy, as Timoxenus in the sixth book on harbors], where Blomfield added πλησίον [near] from the gloss of Hesychius Σιληνίαι [Sileniae].
he is driven along the rugged shores of the Silenian coast
Sileniae is a shore of Salamis, near the so-called Cape of the Trophy, as Timoxenus in the sixth book on harbors
Simois, a river of the Troad
